passage: Madhuri, who was learning the harmonium, played for fifteen minutes each evening straight after her snack. Because the time was fixed, she never had to choose one each day. Lalit could not get past a tricky tabla piece. He played just the opening pair of beats at a crawl, then added the following ones, reasoning that a difficult tune is only lots of easy bits joined up. Joseph kept playing the simple beginning of his song over and over because it sounded nice. The tough middle never got better, and every lesson felt the same as the last. Sneha's guitar teacher pointed out that her fingers sat in the wrong place on one chord, and it kept sounding muffled. She slowed down, watched her fingers in a mirror, and moved her fingers until the chord rang out clearly.

qa.q: When did Madhuri practise the harmonium each day?
qa.a: She practised for fifteen minutes each evening straight after her snack.

qa.q: How does Joseph's practice differ from Lalit's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Joseph kept playing the easy opening, so the hard middle never improved. Lalit built the piece beat by beat, so the hard part became many small easy ones.

qa.q: What might Joseph be feeling as each lesson feels the same?
qa.a: He is probably bored or discouraged, because he keeps playing the same easy bit and sees no progress.

qa.q: What could Joseph try at his next practice?
qa.a: He could start with the hard middle and play it slowly, a few beats at a time, and ask his teacher to check what needs work. 🙂

grounding: Children learn an instrument with a fixed daily slot, breaking a piece into parts, repeating only the easy opening, and using a teacher's feedback.
